title: "Unit 3 — Reconstructing Abbreviated or Omitted Proofs"
subtitle: "From a detected gap to a minimal, auditable argument"
description: "A practice unit on freezing a target, auditing quantifiers and domains, constructing a dependency graph, retrieving the right lemmas, and honestly closing or reporting proof gaps."
---

## Learning outcomes {#o017-u03-outcomes}

This unit has the stable identifier **O017-U03**. After completing it, you
will be able to:

1. freeze the claim to be reconstructed without silently adding or removing
   hypotheses;
2. expand the quantifiers, domains, and definitions that determine the form
   of the proof target;
3. turn an abbreviated passage of a proof into a list of obligations with
   clear inputs and outputs;
4. draw a dependency graph connecting the target, lemmas, definitions, and
   hypotheses;
5. retrieve a lemma by its mathematical contract, then check every one of
   its hypotheses in the context you are reading;
6. bring forward planning from the hypotheses together with backward
   planning from the conclusion;
7. write a minimally sufficient reconstruction—complete enough to audit,
   without turning a single step into a new textbook; and
8. distinguish gaps that have been closed, gaps conditional on a reference,
   and gaps that remain unresolved.

::: {.callout-note title="Prerequisites and scope"}
Unit 1 introduced reconstruction by separating an argument into definitions,
assumptions, claims, justifications, and open tasks. Unit 2 taught how to
identify the source and version being read. Unit 3 develops that practice
systematically: types and quantifiers are frozen, obligations are organized
into a dependency graph, lemmas are retrieved through their contracts, and
details are tested through a minimality audit. The D–A–K–J–T labels and the
minimum spanning tree case from Unit 1 are not taught again here.

Readers are assumed to know functions, sets, preimages, topological spaces,
continuity, and the definition of compactness through open covers. All case
excerpts are synthetic material created for this unit.
:::

```{=latex}
\Needspace{6\baselineskip}
```

## The reconstruction problem: not guessing the author's intention {#o017-u03-reconstruction-problem}

Consider the following synthetic excerpt.

> Let $K$ be compact and $f:X\to Y$ continuous. Every open cover of
> $f[K]$ pulls back to an open cover of $K$. Take a finite subcover;
> its image gives a finite subcover of $f[K]$. Hence $f[K]$ is
> compact.

The excerpt points toward a correct theorem, but several of its verbs hide
work:

- what an “open cover of $f[K]$” means, and in which space each set is
  open;
- why the preimages are open;
- why the preimages cover $K$, rather than necessarily covering all of
  $X$;
- which finite set of indices compactness produces;
- why the original sets with **the same indices** cover $f[K]$; and
- what “its image” means, given that the equation
  $f[f^{-1}[V]]=V$ does not hold for a general function.

Reconstruction is not an attempt to write a proof that might roughly have
been intended. It is the construction of an argument in which every addition
can answer two questions: **why is this step needed**, and **what warrants
its use**? If the second answer is not yet available, the step remains
recorded as a gap; it must not be conjured into a new hypothesis.

## A seven-stage protocol {#o017-u03-seven-stage-protocol}

Use the following protocol whenever a source skips a line or a whole page
of proof. The output of each stage becomes the input to the next.

### Stage 1 — Freeze the claim and context {#o017-u03-stage-freeze}

Copy or faithfully paraphrase:

- the target claim;
- every applicable hypothesis, including those stated at the start of the
  section;
- local definitions and notational conventions;
- locators for the beginning and end of the gap; and
- the version of the source being checked.

Separate the visible text from the reader's interpretation. For example, if
the page says “$K$ is compact” but does not say “$K$ is nonempty”, do not
add nonemptiness just because the proof you have in mind wants to choose a
point in $K$.

### Stage 2 — Expand the target's quantifiers, domains, and definitions {#o017-u03-stage-quantifiers}

Write down the type of every object and expand the definition of the
**conclusion** first. This reveals the form of the witness that must be
constructed. To prove compactness, for example, saying “take a cover” is not
enough. The reader must take an arbitrary open cover and produce a finite
index set that still covers the correct object.

This audit also checks for shifts of domain. If $f:X\to Y$ and $V\subseteq Y$,
then $f^{-1}[V]\subseteq X$; the expression $f[V]$ is not even well-typed
unless $V\subseteq X$. Many abbreviated proofs fail not because their
central idea is wrong, but because an object moves between spaces without
justification.

### Stage 3 — State the proof obligations {#o017-u03-stage-obligations}

Replace words such as *clearly*, *similarly*, *pull back*, or *the result
follows* with a numbered list. A good obligation has:

- inputs that are already available;
- an output needed by the next step; and
- a checkable completion criterion.

“Explain preimages” is too vague. “For every $i$, prove that
$f^{-1}[V_i]$ is open in $X$” has a definite output.

### Stage 4 — Construct a dependency graph {#o017-u03-stage-dependency-graph}

Create a node for the target, each obligation, each active hypothesis, and
each lemma that might be used. Draw arrows from inputs to the conclusion
that depends on them. The graph prevents two mistakes:

1. using a conclusion before its supporting nodes have been closed; and
2. proving an interesting result with no path to the target.

Leaf nodes must be hypotheses, definitions, already-proved results, or
retrievable references. “A well-known theorem” is not an auditable leaf node.

### Stage 5 — Retrieve lemmas through their contracts {#o017-u03-stage-lemma-retrieval}

Do not start with a lemma's name alone. Write down the **contract** you need:

```text
inputs + hypotheses  ──>  output
```

Then match candidate lemmas against that contract, word by word. Record the
exact statement, domain, all hypotheses, and its locator. Make an
instantiation table explaining which object in the current case corresponds
to each object in the lemma. A lemma has not been “retrieved” if you have
found its name but have not checked one of its hypotheses.

If a small result can be proved directly in one or two lines, a local proof
is often more auditable than a vague reference. If the result is substantive,
use a precise reference; do not copy its conclusion while dropping its
conditions.

### Stage 6 — Plan backward and forward {#o017-u03-stage-bidirectional-planning}

**Backward** planning asks: for the conclusion to hold, what object or
property must be available immediately beforehand? **Forward** planning asks:
what follows directly from the hypotheses and definitions? A reconstruction
is usually found where these two directions meet.

A plan is not a proof. The arrow “compactness of $K$ $\Rightarrow$ finite
index set” is valid only after its input family has been shown to be an open
cover of $K$.

### Stage 7 — Write a minimally sufficient reconstruction and audit what remains {#o017-u03-stage-minimal-proof}

Write the proof in a natural reading order. Then perform two tests.

- **Deletion test:** if a sentence is removed, does an important arrow in
  the graph lose its justification? If not, the sentence may be unnecessary.
- **Gap test:** does every remaining arrow lead back to a definition,
  hypothesis, local proof, or lemma with a matching contract?

Record each gap's status as `closed`, `conditional`, `unconfirmed`, or
`rejected`. “Minimal” does not mean as short as possible. It means that no
essential obligation is hidden and no additional theory is brought in
without a purpose.

## A reconstruction worksheet {#o017-u03-reconstruction-sheet}

The following single sheet is usually enough to contain the entire process.

::: {.o017-table-scroll aria-label="Proof reconstruction worksheet" tabindex="0"}
| Field | Auditable content |
|---|---|
| Frozen claim | the statement, hypotheses, and context that are actually available |
| Object dictionary | symbols, domains, and inclusion or mapping relationships |
| Target form | the definition of the conclusion with explicit quantifiers |
| Obligations | a list of small outputs to construct |
| Graph | dependency arrows and leaf nodes |
| Lemma contracts | inputs, hypotheses, outputs, locators, instantiations |
| Two-way plan | forward path, backward path, and meeting point |
| Reconstruction | a sequential proof that closes the graph |
| Gap register | status, basis for that status, and action still needed |
| Claim boundary | what is deliberately not concluded |
:::

This sheet is a logical working record, not the full provenance logbook
that is the focus of Unit 4. Nevertheless, a lemma retrieved from a source
still needs enough version identity and locator information to be checked.

## Worked case: the continuous image of a compact set {#o017-u03-worked-case}

We now apply all seven stages to the opening excerpt. This case deliberately
uses the open-cover definition, rather than sequential criteria,
Heine–Borel, or the extreme value theorem. Every shift of quantifier and
domain is therefore visible.

### Freezing the statement {#o017-u03-frozen-statement}

::: {#thm-o017-u03-compact-image .theorem title="The continuous image of a compact set"}
Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces, let $K\subseteq X$ be compact, and
let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous. Then the image

$$
f[K]=\{f(x):x\in K\}
$$

is compact in $Y$.
:::

This frozen statement does not assume that $K$ is nonempty, that $f$ is
injective, that $f$ is surjective onto $Y$, or that $Y$ is Hausdorff. A
reconstruction using any of these four properties would strengthen the
source's hypotheses without justification.

In this unit, “$K$ is compact in $X$” means: for every family
$(U_i)_{i\in I}$ of sets open in $X$ satisfying
$K\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$, there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ such that
$K\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in F}U_i$. This definition is equivalent to compactness
of $K$ in the subspace topology, but that equivalence is not needed in this
reconstruction.

### Auditing quantifiers and domains {#o017-u03-quantifier-domain-audit}

The conclusion “$f[K]$ is compact in $Y$” expands to:

::: {.o017-math-scroll aria-label="Explicit quantifiers for compactness of the image" tabindex="0"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{for every index set }I\text{ and family }(V_i)_{i\in I},\\
&\left[\bigl(\forall i\in I,\;V_i\text{ is open in }Y\bigr)
\land f[K]\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i\right]\\
&\qquad\Longrightarrow
\left[\exists F\subseteq I,\;F\text{ is finite and }
f[K]\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in F}V_i\right].
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

The object dictionary is as follows.

::: {.o017-table-scroll aria-label="Object dictionary for the compact-image proof" tabindex="0"}
| Symbol | Domain or type | Role |
|---|---|---|
| $x$ | an element of $X$, later restricted to $K$ | witness on the domain side |
| $y$ | an element of $Y$, later restricted to $f[K]$ | element to be covered |
| $i$ | an element of an arbitrary index set $I$ | identifies a member of the cover |
| $V_i$ | an open set in $Y$ | member of the original cover |
| $U_i=f^{-1}[V_i]$ | a subset of $X$ | candidate member of the pullback cover |
| $F$ | a finite subset of $I$ | witness for a finite subcover |
:::

The quantifier order matters. The family $(V_i)$ is first chosen
arbitrarily; only then may $F$ depend on that family. Choosing one $F$ before
the cover is known would prove a much stronger and usually false statement.

### List of obligations {#o017-u03-obligations}

The abbreviated excerpt yields five obligations.

1. **P1 — Openness.** For every $i\in I$, prove that
   $U_i=f^{-1}[V_i]$ is open in $X$.
2. **P2 — Backward covering.** Prove that
   $K\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$.
3. **P3 — Applying compactness.** From P1 and P2, produce a finite
   $F\subseteq I$ with
   $K\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in F}U_i$.
4. **P4 — Forward covering.** Using the same index set $F$, prove that
   $f[K]\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in F}V_i$.
5. **P5 — Closing the quantifiers.** Since the original cover was arbitrary,
   conclude that every open cover of $f[K]$ has a finite subcover.

P1 and P2 are different: a family can consist of open sets without covering
$K$, or cover $K$ without consisting of open sets. Compactness can be used
only after both properties are available.

### Dependency graph {#o017-u03-compact-image-graph}

Read the following graph from left to right. Square brackets indicate nodes
that must have an independent justification.

```text
[D1: U_i := f^{-1}[V_i]]
[V_i open in Y] + [f continuous] + D1
    └─> P1: U_i open in X ─────────────────────────────────┐
                                                           │
[V_i cover f[K]] + [definition of f[K]] +                  │
[D2: x ∈ U_i ⇔ f(x) ∈ V_i] + D1                            │
    └─> P2: the family U_i covers K ───────────────────────┤
                                                           v
[K compact] + P1 + P2 ──> P3: there is a finite F ⊆ I      │
                                                           v
P3 + [definition of f[K]] + D1 + D2                        │
    └─> P4: the family V_i, i ∈ F, covers f[K]             │
                                                           │
[arbitrary original cover] + P4 ──> P5: f[K] compact <──────┘
```

The graph also shows what is **not** needed: boundedness of $K$, closedness
of $K$, the Hausdorff property of $Y$, or existence of a maximum. None has
a necessary path to P5.

### Contracts for the results actually needed {#o017-u03-needed-lemmas}

This reconstruction requires one definitional clause and two microlemmas.
No major theorem needs to be retrieved.

::: {.o017-table-scroll aria-label="Microlemma contracts for the compact-image proof" tabindex="0"}
| Working ID | Contract | Basis and how to close it |
|---|---|---|
| C1 | $f$ continuous + $V$ open in $Y$ $\Rightarrow f^{-1}[V]$ open in $X$ | a clause in the definition of continuity |
| L1 | $f[K]\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i$ $\Rightarrow K\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I}f^{-1}[V_i]$ | prove elementwise by taking $x\in K$ |
| L2 | $K\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in F}f^{-1}[V_i]$ $\Rightarrow f[K]\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in F}V_i$ | prove elementwise by taking $y\in f[K]$ and a witness $x\in K$ |
:::

For C1, the instantiation is $V\mapsto V_i$ for every $i\in I$. L1 and L2
require neither injectivity nor surjectivity. Both are deliberately proved
locally below, because their elementwise proofs are shorter and clearer
than an unlocated reference to “properties of images and preimages”.

The identity

$$
f^{-1}\!\left[\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i\right]
=\bigcup_{i\in I}f^{-1}[V_i]
$$

can replace the elementwise proof of L1, but it is not mandatory. If that
identity is retrieved as a lemma, its contract and the domain
$V_i\subseteq Y$ must still be checked.

### Two-way planning {#o017-u03-two-way-plan}

The backward plan starts from the target:

```text
f[K] compact
< need: every open cover of f[K] has a finite subcover
< need: a finite F that still covers f[K]
< candidate producer of F: compactness of K
< need: an open cover of K with the same index set I
```

The forward plan starts from the data:

```text
V_i open + f continuous
> f^{-1}[V_i] open

V_i cover f[K] + x ∈ K
> f(x) ∈ some V_i
> x ∈ some f^{-1}[V_i]
> the preimage family covers K

open cover of K + K compact
> there is a finite F
```

The meeting point of the two plans is the sentence: “the family
$(f^{-1}[V_i])_{i\in I}$ is an open cover of $K$.” After that point,
compactness produces $F$; L2 carries $F$ back to the target.

### Complete reconstruction {#o017-u03-complete-reconstruction}

::: {#prf-o017-u03-compact-image .proof}
Take an index set $I$ and an arbitrary family $(V_i)_{i\in I}$ of open
sets in $Y$ that covers $f[K]$:

$$
f[K]\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i.
$$

For each $i\in I$, set $U_i=f^{-1}[V_i]$. Since $f$ is continuous and
$V_i$ is open in $Y$, the set $U_i$ is open in $X$.

The family $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ covers $K$. Indeed, if $x\in K$, then
$f(x)\in f[K]$. Since $(V_i)_{i\in I}$ covers $f[K]$, there is an $i\in I$
such that $f(x)\in V_i$. By the definition of preimage,
$x\in f^{-1}[V_i]=U_i$.

Compactness of $K$ now applies to this open cover. Thus there is a finite
$F\subseteq I$ such that

$$
K\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in F}U_i
=\bigcup_{i\in F}f^{-1}[V_i].
$$

The family $(V_i)_{i\in F}$ covers $f[K]$. To see this, take
$y\in f[K]$. By the definition of image, there is an $x\in K$ with
$y=f(x)$. Since the family indexed by $F$ covers $K$, there is an $i\in F$
such that $x\in f^{-1}[V_i]$. Hence $y=f(x)\in V_i$.

We have therefore obtained a finite subcover from every arbitrary open cover
of $f[K]$. Thus $f[K]$ is compact in $Y$.
:::

The proof remains valid when $K=\varnothing$. In the final elementwise
paragraph, “take $y\in f[K]$” occurs inside the proof of a universally
quantified implication; there is no $y$ to choose if $f[K]$ is empty. We
do not need to add a nonemptiness hypothesis.

### Why this reconstruction is minimal but sufficient {#o017-u03-minimality-audit}

::: {.o017-table-scroll aria-label="Minimality audit of the compact-image reconstruction" tabindex="0"}
| Part | Arrow closed | Consequence of deleting it |
|---|---|---|
| the original cover is chosen arbitrarily | opens the quantifier in the definition of compactness | the proof handles only one particular cover |
| continuity gives openness of the preimages | P1 | compactness of $K$ is applied to a family not yet shown to be open |
| the argument with $x\in K$ | P2/L1 | the preimages have not been shown to cover $K$ |
| the application of compactness | P3 | there is no finite witness $F$ |
| the argument with $y\in f[K]$ | P4/L2 | the same indices have not been shown to cover the image |
| closing “every cover” | P5 | the compactness conclusion does not yet follow explicitly |
:::

Conversely, the proof need not prove the Heine–Borel theorem, replace covers
with sequences, or show that $f[K]$ is closed. Adding all of that lengthens
the text without closing a new arrow in the graph.

## Invalid shortcuts {#o017-u03-invalid-shortcuts}

### A cover of the image is not a cover of the entire codomain or domain {#o017-u03-cover-scope-error}

From
$f[K]\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i$ it does not follow that
$Y=\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i$. Consequently, it does not follow that the preimages
cover all of $X$ either.

Take $X=Y=\mathbb{R}$, $K=\{0\}$, and let $f$ be the identity function. The
single set $V=(-1,1)$ covers $f[K]$, but $V$ does not cover $Y$ and
$f^{-1}[V]=(-1,1)$ does not cover $X$. The proof needs only the preimages
to cover $K$; demanding a cover of $X$ would create a spurious obligation.

### The image of a preimage does not always recover the original set {#o017-u03-image-preimage-error}

For a general function, the correct identity is

$$
f[f^{-1}[V]]=V\cap f[X],
$$

not $f[f^{-1}[V]]=V$. If $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is given by
$f(x)=0$ and $V=(-1,1)$, then
$f[f^{-1}[V]]=\{0\}\neq V$.

In the main reconstruction, we do not need to equate the two sets. We only
use the implication
$x\in f^{-1}[V_i]\Rightarrow f(x)\in V_i$ for a witness
$x\in K$. This is why the abbreviated phrase “its image gives a subcover”
needs to be replaced by the elementwise argument L2.

### Openness does not transfer without checking the space {#o017-u03-openness-domain-error}

If $V_i$ is open in $Y$, continuity makes $f^{-1}[V_i]$ open in
$X$; it does not say that $V_i$ is open in $X$. If the available function
is only $f|_K:K\to Y$, its preimages are open in the **subspace $K$**, not
automatically in $X$. That version of the theorem can still be proved using
the definition of subspace compactness, but its contract and domains are
different. The reconstruction must follow the version the source actually
states.

## Testing hypotheses with counterexamples {#o017-u03-assumption-stress-tests}

A counterexample does not replace a reconstruction. It tests whether a
hypothesis used in the graph really performs the work claimed for it.

### Without compactness of the domain {#o017-u03-counterexample-noncompact}

The inclusion map

$$
j:(0,1)\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R},\qquad j(x)=x,
$$

is continuous, but its image $(0,1)$ is not compact. The family

$$
U_n=(1/n,1),\qquad n\geq2,
$$

covers $(0,1)$. The empty subfamily clearly does not cover $(0,1)$. Every
nonempty finite subfamily is contained in a single $(1/N,1)$ for the largest
chosen index $N$, and therefore misses, for example, $1/(2N)$. Hence there
is no finite subcover. This example breaks the arrow from P1+P2 to P3:
without compactness, the open cover does not produce $F$.

### Without continuity {#o017-u03-counterexample-discontinuous}

Take

$$
K=\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\in\mathbb{N},\ n\geq1\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}.
$$

The set $K$ is compact by the open-cover definition. For any cover, choose
a member containing $0$. Because that member is open, it contains $1/n$
for all sufficiently large $n$; only finitely many points remain, and one
member of the original cover can be chosen for each remaining point.

Define $g:K\to\mathbb{R}$ by $g(0)=0$ and $g(1/n)=n$. This function is
not continuous at $0$: the preimage
$g^{-1}[(-1/2,1/2)]=\{0\}$ is not open in $K$, because every neighborhood
of $0$ in $K$ contains $1/n$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Moreover,

$$
g[K]=\{0,1,2,3,\ldots\}
$$

is not compact. The family $W_m=(-1,m)$, $m\geq1$, covers $g[K]$, but every
finite subfamily misses all sufficiently large integers. Here the failure
of continuity breaks P1: preimages of cover members are not guaranteed to
be open.

These two examples also prevent a reconstruction from silently discarding
a hypothesis merely because the abbreviated proof no longer mentions it.

## Retrieving lemmas and rejecting hidden hypotheses {#o017-u03-lemma-audit}

A result's name is often broader than its actual contract. Suppose that,
after the main theorem, a source adds:

> Since $f[K]$ is compact, $f[K]$ is closed in $Y$.

The candidate result readers commonly recall has the contract:

::: {.o017-math-scroll aria-label="Contract for the lemma on compact sets in a Hausdorff space" tabindex="0"}
$$
\bigl(Y\text{ is Hausdorff}\bigr)
\land\bigl(C\subseteq Y\bigr)
\land\bigl(C\text{ is compact}\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C\text{ is closed in }Y.
$$
:::

This contract can be proved locally. If $C=\varnothing$, the conclusion
is immediate. If $C\neq\varnothing$, take $y\in Y\setminus C$. For every
$x\in C$, the Hausdorff property gives disjoint open sets $U_x$ and
$V_x$ with $x\in U_x$ and $y\in V_x$. The family $(U_x)_{x\in C}$ covers
$C$; since $C$ is compact, there are $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in C$ such that
$C\subseteq U_{x_1}\cup\cdots\cup U_{x_n}$. The set
$V=V_{x_1}\cap\cdots\cap V_{x_n}$ is open, contains $y$, and is disjoint
from $U_{x_1}\cup\cdots\cup U_{x_n}$, so $V\subseteq Y\setminus C$.
Thus every point in $Y\setminus C$ has a neighborhood contained in
$Y\setminus C$; the complement of $C$ is open and $C$ is closed.

Its instantiation table must take the following form.

::: {.o017-table-scroll aria-label="Instantiating the compact-implies-closed lemma" tabindex="0"}
| Lemma variable | Instantiation | Hypothesis status |
|---|---|---|
| ambient space $Y$ | $Y$ in the main theorem | available as a topological space |
| $Y$ Hausdorff | no counterpart in the frozen statement | **not yet available** |
| set $C$ | $f[K]$ | available |
| $C$ compact | result of the main reconstruction | available |
| conclusion $C$ closed | $f[K]$ closed in $Y$ | additional target |
:::

The contract does not match because the Hausdorff condition is unavailable.
This is not merely formal caution; the additional conclusion is genuinely
false in general.

Take the Sierpiński space
$Y=\{0,1\}$ with topology
$\{\varnothing,\{1\},Y\}$. Let $X=K=\{*\}$ have the one-point topology,
and let $f:K\to Y$ be given by $f(*)=1$. The set $K$ is compact. The
function $f$ is continuous because the preimages of the three open sets
in $Y$ are each either $\varnothing$ or $K$, which are open in $K$. Its
image $\{1\}$ is also compact, but it is not closed in $Y$, because its
complement $\{0\}$ is not open.

If an earlier page of the source might stipulate that all spaces are
Hausdorff, an honest note is not “Hausdorff is surely assumed”, but:

::: {.o017-table-scroll aria-label="Gap register for the Hausdorff hypothesis" tabindex="0"}
| Gap ID | Claim | Status | Basis | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G-H | $Y$ Hausdorff holds in the context | unconfirmed | absent from the frozen excerpt | check the context and source version |
| G-C | $f[K]$ closed in $Y$ | rejected as a standalone claim; conditional on G-H | lemma contract and Sierpiński example | add the condition only if supported by the source |
:::

Lemma retrieval has three possible outcomes:

1. all hypotheses match, so the node can be closed;
2. a hypothesis cannot yet be found, so the node remains open; or
3. a hypothesis contradicts the context or there is a counterexample, so
   that path is rejected.

Only the first outcome warrants proceeding as though the lemma has been
applied.

## Choosing minimally sufficient detail {#o017-u03-detail-level}

The level of detail depends on what is already available to the intended
reader, not on the reconstruction writer's preferences. Use the following
decision sequence.

1. If a step is definitional but shifts a quantifier or domain, write its
   instantiation. In the main case, C1 needs to be stated because it
   produces openness in the correct space.
2. If a step is a microlemma forming a principal bridge, prove it
   elementwise. L1 and L2 each require just one witness.
3. If a substantive lemma is already available in the same source, cite
   the result's number and check its hypotheses; do not copy its entire
   proof.
4. If a substantive lemma is not yet available, retrieve a traceable source
   or mark the gap. Do not fill the absence with a theorem name without
   a contract.
5. If a paragraph supports no path in the graph, move it to a supplementary
   note or remove it from the core reconstruction.

A minimal reconstruction also preserves the **exact strength** of the
source's claim. The main theorem proves compactness of $f[K]$; it does
not prove that $f[K]$ is closed, bounded, or has a maximum point in every
codomain. Those conclusions require additional structure and lemmas.

::: {.callout-important title="Reconstruction stopping rule"}
Stop when every path to the frozen claim has been closed and every other
gap has a status. Do not expand the work to prove every neighboring result.
Conversely, do not declare completion merely because the central idea looks
right if an arrow involving a domain, quantifier, or hypothesis still lacks
justification.
:::

## A short audit exercise {#o017-u03-short-audit}

A reader offers the following reconstruction of the main excerpt:

> Take a cover $(V_i)$ of $f[K]$. Since $f$ is continuous, every $f[V_i]$
> is open in $Y$. These sets cover $K$. Compactness of $Y$ gives finitely
> many indices, so we are done.

A type audit immediately finds three defects before we assess the
central idea.

- $V_i\subseteq Y$, whereas the domain of $f$ is $X$; $f[V_i]$ is not
  well-typed in general. The required object is $f^{-1}[V_i]\subseteq X$.
- The preimage family must be proved to cover $K$, not simply declared
  to do so.
- The compactness hypothesis belongs to $K$, not $Y$.

After these repairs, a step carrying the finite subcover back to $f[K]$
is still needed. Finding the first three errors does not, by itself,
close P4.

## Exercises {#o017-u03-exercises}

1. **[O017-U03-X01]{#o017-u03-x01} — Quantifier audit.** Write the quantified
   form of “$f[K]$ is compact” and explain why the finite index set $F$ may
   depend on the cover $(V_i)_{i\in I}$, but not conversely.
2. **[O017-U03-X02]{#o017-u03-x02} — Dependency graph.** Without looking at
   the worked-case graph, construct a minimal graph from an open cover of
   $f[K]$ to the compactness conclusion. Mark what is closed by definitions,
   continuity, compactness, L1, and L2.
3. **[O017-U03-X03]{#o017-u03-x03} — A false shortcut.** Give a concrete
   example refuting $f[f^{-1}[V]]=V$. State the correct identity and explain
   why the main proof requires only one direction of implication.
4. **[O017-U03-X04]{#o017-u03-x04} — Testing hypotheses.** Construct or
   explain one example with a noncompact domain and another with a
   discontinuous function for which the image is not compact. Connect each
   failure to a node in the graph.
5. **[O017-U03-X05]{#o017-u03-x05} — Lemma contract.** Audit the sentence
   “$f[K]$ is compact, so $f[K]$ is closed in $Y$.” Write the required
   lemma contract, the missing hypothesis, and an honest gap status when
   the earlier context cannot yet be checked.
6. **[O017-U03-X06]{#o017-u03-x06} — Minimal repair.** Repair the excerpt in
   the Short audit exercise section. Make a three-column table containing
   the faulty fragment, the type of defect, and a minimal replacement;
   then add the originally missing P4 step.

## Hints and answer guidance {#o017-u03-guidance}

1. **[O017-U03-H01]{#o017-u03-h01}.** The order is: for every $I$ and every
   open family $(V_i)_{i\in I}$ covering $f[K]$, there is a finite
   $F\subseteq I$ that still covers $f[K]$. Since $F$ is a witness for
   the chosen cover, it comes after the family quantifier.
2. **[O017-U03-H02]{#o017-u03-h02}.** The minimal path is the original cover
   $\to$ open preimages (continuity) and preimages covering $K$ (L1)
   $\to$ finite indices (compactness of $K$) $\to$ the same indices covering
   $f[K]$ (L2) $\to$ the definition of compactness.
3. **[O017-U03-H03]{#o017-u03-h03}.** Use the constant function
   $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)=0$, and $V=(-1,1)$. The correct
   identity is $f[f^{-1}[V]]=V\cap f[X]$. P4 uses only
   $x\in f^{-1}[V]\Rightarrow f(x)\in V$.
4. **[O017-U03-H04]{#o017-u03-h04}.** The inclusion
   $j:(0,1)\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ breaks the step from an open cover
   to a finite subcover. The function
   $g(0)=0$, $g(1/n)=n$ on $\{0\}\cup\{1/n\}$ breaks the step guaranteeing
   openness of the preimages.
5. **[O017-U03-H05]{#o017-u03-h05}.** The valid contract requires $Y$ to be
   Hausdorff and $f[K]$ to be compact. Without a basis for $Y$ being
   Hausdorff, the application is `unconfirmed`; as a standalone claim it
   is refuted by the Sierpiński example. Do not add Hausdorff to the frozen
   statement.
6. **[O017-U03-H06]{#o017-u03-h06}.** Replace $f[V_i]$ with
   $f^{-1}[V_i]$, prove that the family covers $K$, and apply compactness
   of $K$, not $Y$. For P4, take $y\in f[K]$, choose $x\in K$ with
   $y=f(x)$, then use membership of $x$ in one of the finitely indexed
   preimages.

## Unit completion task {#o017-u03-completion-task}

Reconstruct the following synthetic excerpt as a **proof dossier**.

> If $K$ is compact and $F$ is closed in $K$, then $F$ is compact. Indeed,
> add the complement of $F$ to a cover of $F$, apply compactness of $K$,
> then discard the complement.

Use the convention that $K$ is a compact topological space, $F\subseteq K$
is closed, and compactness of $F$ is tested with families of sets open in
$K$ and covering $F$.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{5\baselineskip}
```

The dossier must contain:

1. the frozen claim, quantifier order, and a domain dictionary for $K$,
   $F$, the family $(U_i)_{i\in I}$, the complement $K\setminus F$, and
   the finite index set;
2. a list of obligations replacing “add”, “apply”, and “discard”;
3. a dependency graph whose leaf nodes all have a justification;
4. the contract and instantiation of the clause “$F$ is closed in $K$ if
   and only if $K\setminus F$ is open in $K$”;
5. backward and forward plans and their meeting point;
6. a minimal proof that handles the possibility that the finite subcover
   of $K$ does not select $K\setminus F$;
7. a deletion test for at least four proof sentences;
8. a gap register with final statuses; and
9. one claim boundary: explain why this proof does not by itself show that
   $F$ is closed in an ambient space larger than $K$.

### Rubric {#o017-u03-completion-rubric}

Score each criterion 0, 1, or 2.

::: {.o017-table-scroll aria-label="Unit 3 completion task rubric" tabindex="0"}
| Criterion | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claim and domains | hypotheses or spaces change | some types or quantifiers remain implicit | all objects, quantifiers, and ambient-space topologies are correct |
| Obligations and graph | principal leaps remain hidden | a graph exists but has unjustified leaves | every abbreviated verb becomes an obligation and every path is closed |
| Lemma contract | the lemma is merely named | a contract exists but instantiation is incomplete | inputs, hypotheses, outputs, and instantiation are checked |
| Reconstruction | the argument does not produce a finite subcover of $F$ | the idea is correct with one unjustified transition | a complete elementwise proof handles both possibilities for selecting the complement |
| Minimal but sufficient | too abbreviated or introduces irrelevant theory | some sentences remain untested | the deletion test shows that every core detail has a purpose |
| Honesty about gaps and boundaries | gaps are hidden or the claim is strengthened | statuses or boundaries are named without a basis | all gaps have grounded statuses and the conclusion about the ambient space is correctly bounded |
:::

A passing score is at least 10 out of 12, with a score of 2 for
**Reconstruction** and **Honesty about gaps and boundaries**. Adding a
hypothesis that is absent, using compactness before the family has been
proved to be an open cover, or declaring a gap closed on the basis of a
lemma's name alone requires revision even if the total score is sufficient.

## Boundary with B80 and other units {#o017-u03-boundary}

This unit teaches logical reconstruction, not computational skills. It does
not teach Python syntax, SageMath, SymPy, NumPy/SciPy, package APIs, numerical
methods, plotting, writing tests, notebooks, software environments, or the
implementation differences between exact and floating-point numbers. All
of those belong to B80.

Readers who already have B80 skills may use programs to search for examples
or test conjectures during reconstruction. Their output remains diagnostic
empirical evidence, not a substitute for a proof path in the graph. This
unit also does not reteach version tracing from Unit 2, the full provenance
logbook from Unit 4, or computational reproducibility from Unit 6. If lemma
retrieval uncovers a source problem, record that need and pass it on to the
appropriate unit.
